ts13_name.topic: The name Israel in the record: Merneptah Stele, Genesis 32, Hosea 12, philology

claims.text: Britannica: Merneptah set up the stela after defeating a Libyan invasion around 1209 BCE; it 'contains the earliest-known reference to Israel', which Merneptah counted among the peoples he defeated.

Merneptah Stele: c. 1208 BCE, Merneptah's 5th regnal year; found by Flinders Petrie at Thebes in 1896; black granite, over 3 m, 28 lines, carved on the back of a stele of Amenhotep III; Egyptian Museum Cairo JE 31408; line 27 'Israel is laid waste—its seed is no more'; Israel written with the determinative for a people (seated man and woman), not the city/land determinative used for Ashkelon, Gezer, Yanoam; majority read it as Israel, minority readings Jezreel and 'wearers of the sidelock'.

Etymology: el ('God') with a verb read as sarah ('contend, persist, persevere') or sarar ('rule, prevail'); traditional 'he struggles with God'; John Day: probably 'El will rule'; Mark S. Smith: the name is El-based, not Yahwistic, 'El was the original chief god of the group named Israel'; Eblaite and Ugaritic forms attested.

Genesis 32:24–31 (ESV): Jacob left alone, 'a man wrestled with him until the breaking of the day'; hip put out of joint; 'I will not let you go unless you bless me'; renamed 'Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed'; 'I have seen God face to face'; 'The sun rose upon him as he passed Penuel, limping'.
Hosea 12:3 (ESV): 'In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and in his manhood he strove with God'; v.4: he strove with the angel and prevailed, wept and sought his favour.
Heiser (2008) notes possible Hebrew roots sarah (struggle), sarar (rule) and yasar (upright) behind the name.

ts13_jacob.topic: Allegorical and mystical readings of Jacob/Israel: Philo, Origen, Kabbalah, Sacks, John of the Cross

claims.text: Philo (Yonge trans.): Jacob had his name changed to Israel; Jacob means 'a supplanter', Israel signifies 'the man who sees God'; the practiser of virtue strives 'acutely and clearly to behold the living God'.

Alesso: Philo gives Israel a new etymology, 'the one who sees God', 'the seeing race', 'the seer', later repeated by the Church Fathers; Platonic echoes in his praise of sight; Philo widens Israel from a nation (ethnos) to a kind (genos), a philosophical category.

Origen: 'as man consists of body, and soul, and spirit, so in the same way does Scripture'; the simple edified by the 'flesh', the advanced by the 'soul', the perfect by the 'spiritual law'; quotes Paul 'Israel after the flesh'; speaks of a 'race of Jews inwardly', bodily Israelites a type of spiritual ones, Jerusalem read as the heavenly city.
Lurianic teaching (Chabad trans.): Jacob corresponds to tiferet, which reconciles chesed and gevurah: 'Jacob reconciles the first two'.
Palvanov: the patriarchs as Chesed (Abraham), Gevurah (Isaac), Tiferet (Jacob); 'Jacob was Tiferet'; cites Micah 7:20 and Zohar Raya Mehemna III 255a (Chesed water, Gevurah fire, Tiferet air).

Tiferet: 'beauty, glory, adornment'; balance and integration of expansive Chesed and restrictive Gevurah; astrological correspondence the sun; centre of Zer Anpin, masculine counterpart of the feminine Malkhut.

Sacks: Jacob that night 'throws off the image of Esau, the person he wants to be' and thereafter 'is content to be himself'; 'We have to be at peace with ourself before we can be at peace with the world'; opponent variously a man, an angel (Hosea), Samael (Sages), God (Jacob).

John of the Cross (1542–1591), cofounder of the Discalced Carmelites, canonized 1726, Doctor of the Church 1926; jailed in Toledo from 3–4 Dec 1577, escaped 15 Aug 1578; the spiritual term 'dark night of the soul' takes its name from his poem, with a prose commentary of the 1580s; the night is the soul's detachment on the way to union with God.
Reused: Scofield (Rom 11 note): 'That the Christian now inherits the distinctive Jewish promises is not taught in Scripture'; ICEJ warns of 'Cloaked versions of Replacement theology'.

ts13_israel_lens.topic: The IS-RA-EL (Isis-Ra-El) reading: proponents traced, philological objections

claims.text: Heiser (30 July 2008) reports that Jordan Maxwell claimed 'Israel' derives from 'three deity names: Isis-Ra-El', calling it 'utter nonsense'; Genesis 32 gives the name's origin and Egyptian and Hebrew belong to different language families.

Heiser: the Egyptian goddess's name was nearer 'Awset'/'Waset', 'Isis' being the Greek form; the 'ra' in Israel is resh+aleph, whereas Egyptian Ra is written with a sign equivalent to ayin (cf. Hophra, Jer 44:30); concedes 'El' (aleph+lamed) is correct. Heiser cites no date or work for Maxwell's claim.

Jordan Maxwell described himself as an 'independent scholar in the field of occult / religious philosophy', interest from 1959; Religion Editor of Truth Seeker; seminars, radio, an 'Ancient Mystery Series'.

Glorian glossary (undated, unattributed) reads IS as recalling 'Isis and the Isiac Mysteries', RA as the Solar Logos, EL as 'the inner, profound God within each one of us', and the people of Israel as parts of the inner being, Egypt as enslavement to the ego.

ts13_mysteries.topic: Documented mystery traditions and ascent patterns; later Egyptian-lineage constructions

claims.text: Apuleius, Metamorphoses (2nd c. CE) 11.23: Lucius 'reached the very gates of death', 'treading Proserpine's threshold', passed through the elements, saw 'the sun at midnight shining brightly', came before gods below and above; reveals only what may be told to the uninitiated.

Corpus Hermeticum written c. 100–300 CE, compiled by Byzantine editors; Ficino interrupted translating Plato for Cosimo de' Medici (1462/3) to translate it; Casaubon in 1614 showed from its Koine Greek that it did not predate Plato; Hermes Trismegistus combines Hermes and Thoth; Mahé suggested Hellenistic Egyptian background.

On the Mysteries, attributed to Iamblichus (attribution first in Proclus), a reply to Porphyry's Letter to Anebo under the name Abammon, 'primarily concerned with ritual and theurgy'; Greek text printed by Aldus, Venice 1497.

Eleusinian Mysteries: 'most famous of the secret religious rites of ancient Greece', based on the Hymn to Demeter; Lesser Mysteries at Agrai, Greater at Eleusis in Boedromion; the rites 'were and remain a secret'; initiate 'promised benefits of some kind in the afterlife'.

Merkabah mysticism: centred on Ezekiel 1 throne-chariot; Hekhalot texts (Hekhalot Rabbati, Zutartey, Maaseh Merkabah, 3 Enoch) redacted after the 3rd and before the 9th century CE; ascent through seven heavens/palaces past guardian angels; practitioners called yordei merkavah, 'descenders to the chariot'; Mishnah Hagigah restricts teaching.
Plato, Symposium 210a–212b: Diotima's lover moves from bodies to souls to institutions and knowledge 'until he catches a glimpse of Beauty itself'.
Plotinian ascent (MacLennan): reverse of emanation; purification, awakening of intellect, union with the One as grace; 'like knows like'; cycle of withdrawal and return.
Upanishads: earliest (Brihadaranyaka to Kena) c. 800–500 BCE; atman part of Brahman; Chandogya 'tat tvam asi', 'Thou Art That'; moksha through realisation.

Jean Terrasson (1670–1750), Sethos (1731), a fantasy novel that 'elided Masonic and ancient Egyptian ritual', inspired Mozart and Schikaneder's Magic Flute; Masonic encyclopedia: 'Under the form of fiction' it describes Egyptian initiation and was 'very freely used by Lenoir, Clavel, Oliver' and other writers.

Cagliostro went to France 1778, founded the Egyptian-themed lodge 'Three Crowned Hearts' at Mitau in 1779; he and the Marquis de Alietta 'invented the legend' of an Egyptian journey; museum calls 18th-century Egyptian rituals 'speculative and cosmetic in nature'.

Rosicrucian manifestos: Fama Fraternitatis printed Kassel 1614, Confessio 1615, Chymical Wedding 1616; Andreae called it a 'ludibrium'; Edighoffer: 'no proof that the Brotherhood... ever existed'; actual Rosicrucian organisations appear only in the 18th century.
AMORC founded by H. Spencer Lewis in the US in 1915; traces its origins to Ancient Egypt and Egyptian pharaohs; considers itself 'a continuation of the ancient mystery schools'.

ts13_deed.topic: Institutional literalism (dispensational land reading) vs inner readings; argument labelled

claims.text: Reused: dispensationalism's core is the Israel/church distinction (Mathison); two plans, an earthly people Israel and a heavenly people the church (Weber); Scofield calls the Abrahamic Covenant 'wholly gracious and unconditional', sets out a 'Palestinian Covenant' ending in restoration to the land, and denies that the Christian 'inherits the distinctive Jewish promises'.

Reused: Hagee 2011 'It is the property of the people of Israel'; covenant with 'Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob'; stated policy: Israelis alone decide on land and peace. LifeWay 2017: 63% of evangelical-belief respondents support Israel because 'God gave the land of Israel to the Jewish people'. Spector: most Christian Zionists do not base support on end-times scenario.
Origen's spiritual 'Israel' sits beside a reading in which bodily Israel is only a 'type'; Philo widens Israel to a genos while keeping it a people bound by God's law.
Reused: ICEJ (4 Mar 2012) warned of 'Cloaked versions of Replacement theology' at the Christ at the Checkpoint conference.
